description: We are a group of teenagers from Indonesia who want to make something useful for our country. By harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS hotspot records, we built a 26-year fire calendar that shows when and where peat fires recur, so that action can be planned before the season rather than after the smoke.
summary:
NASA has flown MODIS since November 2000 at 1 km, and VIIRS since January 2012 at 375 m, seven times less ground area. Each pixel reports an average temperature, so a small fire barely moves a 1 km average but clearly moves a 375 m one. VIIRS therefore registers fires MODIS misses, so stacking the two records produces a false jump at 2012: Central Kalimantan’s raw totals rise from 11,642 to 59,337, while MODIS alone fell.

This matters most on peatland, where fires smoulder below the surface and the heat reaching the surface is faint, exactly the signal a 1 km pixel averages away.

We built a 26-year fire activity calendar for Indonesian peatland as a Streamlit web app, from 7.8 million detections across six regions. Using the 179 months when both sensors ran, we measured MODIS at 0.218 times VIIRS and converted the VIIRS years to MODIS-equivalent, so the years before 2012 stand exactly as recorded. The harmonised record shows 92% of Central Kalimantan’s detections fall in August to October, and that 2026 ranks third worst in 26 years. A village head or district disaster office uses it to decide which areas to patrol first.
details:
THE PROBLEM

NASA has flown MODIS on Terra and Aqua since November 2000, and VIIRS on Suomi NPP since January 2012, joined by NOAA-20 in 2018. A VIIRS pixel covers about seven times less ground area than a MODIS pixel, and each pixel reports the average temperature of that patch of ground. A small fire barely moves the average of a 1 km pixel but clearly moves the average of a 375 m one, so VIIRS registers fires MODIS misses. Stacking the two records therefore produces a false jump at 2012: in Central Kalimantan the raw totals go from 11,642 in 2011 to 59,337 in 2012, while MODIS alone fell slightly. The jump is the sensor changing, not the fires.

WHY PEATLAND

Peat fires smoulder below the surface, so the heat reaching the surface is faint. That faint signal barely shifts the average temperature of a 1 km MODIS pixel and is often missed, while a 375 m VIIRS pixel registers it clearly. Peatland is therefore the land where the gap between the two sensors matters most.

WHAT IT DOES

We built a 26-year fire activity calendar for Indonesian peatland as a Streamlit web app, with five views: harmonised calendar, map, current month, before-versus-after comparison, and raw data. The map offers two styles, single-year and multi-year modes, and a year-by-year animation from 2000 to 2026 with locked scale and camera. It covers six regions: Indonesia, Kalimantan, Central Kalimantan, Sumatra, Riau and Papua. It is built from 7.8 million detection rows across six FIRMS CSV files, combining the archive record with near-real-time data, aggregated to 0.5° cells of roughly 55 km.

HOW IT WORKS

Our method measures the relationship between the two sensors using only months when both were operating: 179 overlapping months. A regression through the origin on grid-cell counts gives MODIS equal to 0.218 × VIIRS. We keep MODIS as the unit, so the years from 2000 to 2011 stand exactly as recorded, and the VIIRS years from 2012 onward are converted to MODIS-equivalent. The same relationship computed independently in Python, by pooling monthly totals in the opposite direction, gives VIIRS at 4.72× MODIS, equivalent to 0.212, agreeing within 3%.

WHAT IT FOUND

The harmonised record shows that 92% of 26 years of detections in Central Kalimantan fall in August, September and October, with September alone accounting for 44%; that 2026 ranks third worst in 26 years; and that ten of the 276 cells which have ever recorded fire, 3.6% of them, account for 23% of all detections.

TOOLS WE USED

The project is built in Python 3.14 and runs on an ordinary laptop. Pandas handles the data aggregation, while Streamlit provides the interface. For visualisation, pydeck renders the map, Plotly produces the interactive charts, and Matplotlib exports the final figures. The code is version-controlled on GitHub and the application is deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud.

AI TOOLS DISCLOSURE

1. Claude (Anthrophic)
2. Gemini (Google)

PURPOSE
Assisting with writing and debugging Python scripts to clean raw NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS CSV datasets, apply coastal/static-source filters, and perform spatial joins across Indonesian provincial boundaries. Also to propose the structure of the status logic, and to assist innovation description and README.

DECISIONS WE MADE

Several decisions shaped how we computed the ratio. We used pooled totals across the months when both sensors were operating, rather than averaging monthly ratios, because quiet months produce extreme ratios that would be weighted as heavily as a peak month such as September. We also chose MODIS as the unit rather than VIIRS, because MODIS covers all 26 years. Keeping it as the unit means the older years stand as measured rather than becoming estimates. The harmonisation factor is fitted on archive data only, which is reprocessed and stable, while the calendar itself includes near-real-time data so the record runs to the current month.

WHY IT MATTERS

Our contribution is a 26-year comparative record of fire detections, which required resolving the sensor change rather than working around it. Fire activity concentrates in August, September and October, and a small number of cells account for a disproportionate share of all detections. Because that concentration persists across the whole record, citizens, government agencies and disaster management offices can decide which areas to patrol first rather than respond only once fires are reported.
